did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with the heading “A prophecy concerning Moab”—a message bearing judgment against Moab. The destruction is described as taking place at night, while Ar and Kir-Moab are also devastated.

Mourning spreads throughout Moab, including the areas of Nebo and Medeba. The people express their grief by shaving their heads and cutting their beards—mourning practices explicitly mentioned in the verse.
The mourning is not merely personal: the people of Moab wear sackcloth, go up onto the rooftops, and take to the streets, where a general wailing is heard.
The cries of Heshbon and Elealeh are heard as far as Jahaz. Even Moab’s armed men—that is, those going to war or prepared for it—raise a cry of anguish.
The prophet describes Moab’s flight through Zoar, Eglath-shelishiyah, and the ascent of Luhith. Along the way, weeping and cries of anguish are heard all the way to the road of Horonaim.
The waters of Nimrim are described as desolate, and the hay, grass, and greenery wither. Thus, the destruction affects not only the cities but also the water sources and vegetation.

As a result of the disaster, possessions—or “the wealth they have acquired”—are carried away to the Valley of the Poplars. The verse therefore describes both the loss of property and its removal to another place.
The wailing surrounds Moab’s territory; it is heard in Eglaim and Beer-elim. This description emphasizes how the disaster has spread throughout the land.
The waters of Dimon are described as filled with blood, and the verse adds a threat to the refugees and the survivors of the land: a lion will attack them as well.
